description_full: AMETEK, Inc. manufactures and sells electronic instruments (EIG) and electromechanical (EMG) devices in the United States and internationally. It operates through EIG and EMG segments. The company offers advanced instruments for the process, aerospace, power, and industrial markets; process and analytical instruments for the oil and gas, petrochemical, pharmaceutical, semiconductor, automation, and food and beverage industries; instruments to the laboratory equipment, ultra-precision manufacturing, medical, and test and measurement markets; power quality monitoring and metering devices, uninterruptible power supplies, programmable power and electromagnetic compatibility test equipment, and gas turbines sensors; dashboard instruments for heavy trucks and other vehicles; instrumentation and controls for food and beverage industries; and aircraft and engine sensors, embedded computing, monitoring, power supplies, fuel and fluid measurement, and data acquisition systems for aerospace and defense industry. It also provides engineered medical components and devices, automation solutions, thermal management systems, specialty metals, and electrical interconnects; single-use and consumable surgical instruments, implantable components, and drug delivery systems; engineered electrical connectors and electronics packaging; precision motion control products for data storage, medical devices, business equipment, automation, and other application; high-purity powdered metals, strips and foils, specialty clad metals, and metal matrix composites; motor-blower systems and heat exchangers for thermal management, military and commercial aircraft, and military ground vehicles; and motors used in commercial appliances, food and beverage machines, hydraulic pumps, and industrial blowers, as well as operates a network of aviation maintenance, repair, and overhaul facilities. AMETEK, Inc. was incorporated in 1930 and is headquartered in Berwyn, Pennsylvania.

financial_summary: AMETEK, Inc. is a large-cap industrials business with a $52.4B market cap on $7.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 9% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $1.7B in free cash flow — roughly 23 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.22× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.8× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 24× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 1.4%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.3× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 26% operating margin runs 17pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.34x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.4% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 29% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 11% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 12% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 24% and a beta of 0.90, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $340.3M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 43% in the 2020 crash, 26% in the 2022 bear market and 53% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $164 (margin of safety -40%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 37%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $125 to $217 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 32.3 vs 23.3, EV/EBITDA 22.0 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 31.4 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 26% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 18 covering analysts target $285 on average, 25% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 9.0%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.09).
It converts 23% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.22x.
ROE of 14% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 3.2% of revenue on R&D and 0.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.8x net debt to EBITDA ($458.0M of cash against $2.3B of debt), with interest covered 23.5x.
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 1.9 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
Goodwill makes up 45% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.4% over 3 years, 10.3% over 5 years and 6.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 6.7% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.05 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 8% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 23%.
Capex runs only 0.3x depreciation (1.8% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 32, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and institutions hold 93%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 2 sales over the past year, net $770K sold.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.4% (0.8% in buybacks and 0.6% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 41 consecutive years, raising it 11.6% a year over the last five.
people: With about 22,500 employees, each generates about $329K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 8.2% a year.
That works out to $74K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.2M (16x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
